We present new predictions for the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) using high-resolution dissipationless cosmological simulations of a flat LCDM Universe which resolve galaxy-size halos and subhalos. We create realistic mock galaxy catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to dark matter halos and subhalos, and we measure the reduced 3PCF as a function of luminosity and color in both real and redshift space. As galaxy luminosity and color are varied, we find small differences in the amplitude and shape dependence of the reduced 3PCF, at a level qualitatively consistent with recent measurements from the SDSS and 2dFGRS. We confirm that discrepancies between previous 3PCF measurements can be explained in part by differences in binning choices. We explore the degree to which a simple local bias model can fit the simulated 3PCF. The agreement between the model predictions and galaxy 3PCF measurements lends further credence to the straightforward association of galaxies with CDM halos and subhalos.

# New Predictions for the Galaxy Three-Point Correlation Function

## Overview

This study presents new theoretical predictions for the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) derived from high-resolution dissipationless cosmological simulations. These simulations model a flat Lambda Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) Universe and are designed to resolve galaxy-size dark matter halos as well as their embedded subhalos, providing the necessary detail to make robust predictions about galaxy clustering on the relevant scales.

## Methodology

To connect the dark matter distribution to observable galaxy populations, we constructed realistic mock galaxy catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to the dark matter halos and subhalos identified in the simulations. This approach enables us to measure the reduced 3PCF as a function of both galaxy luminosity and color, and to do so in both real space and redshift space. By working in both spaces, our predictions can be directly compared with a range of observational measurements.

## Key Findings

Our analysis reveals that varying galaxy luminosity and color produces only small differences in both the amplitude and the shape dependence of the reduced 3PCF. This relative insensitivity is qualitatively consistent with recent measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS), lending confidence to the reliability of our simulation-based approach.

Furthermore, we address the apparent discrepancies that have been reported between previous 3PCF measurements. Our results confirm that these disagreements can be explained, at least in part, by differences in the binning choices adopted in different analyses. This finding highlights the importance of carefully accounting for methodological differences when comparing clustering statistics across studies.

## Implications

The strong agreement between the predictions of the local bias model and the measured galaxy 3PCF provides important physical insight. Specifically, it supports the straightforward association of galaxies with CDM halos and subhalos, suggesting that this simple and physically motivated framework adequately captures the essential features of galaxy clustering at the three-point level. This lends further credence to the standard picture in which galaxies form and reside within the hierarchical structure of dark matter halos.

# New Predictions for the Galaxy Three-Point Correlation Function from Cosmological Simulations

## Introduction and Methodology

Understanding the spatial distribution of galaxies remains one of the central challenges in modern cosmology, offering critical insights into both the underlying dark matter distribution and the physical processes governing galaxy formation. While the two-point correlation function has long served as the workhorse statistic for quantifying galaxy clustering, higher-order statistics such as the three-point correlation function (3PCF) provide complementary information that can break degeneracies and probe the non-Gaussian nature of large-scale structure.

In this study, we present new theoretical predictions for the galaxy 3PCF derived from high-resolution cosmological N-body simulations of a flat Lambda Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) Universe. These simulations resolve the dark matter distribution with sufficient detail to identify not only distinct halos but also the subhalos that survive within larger virialized structures. To bridge the gap between the dark matter distribution and observable galaxy populations, we construct realistic mock catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to individual dark matter halos and subhalos. This approach allows us to directly connect the properties of simulated galaxies with their host dark matter structures.

## Measuring the Reduced Three-Point Correlation Function

Using these mock catalogs, we measure the reduced 3PCF—a normalized quantity that removes the leading-order dependence on the two-point function and thereby isolates the genuine higher-order clustering signal. We examine how this statistic varies as a function of both galaxy luminosity and color, two of the most fundamental observable properties that trace different stages and environments of galaxy evolution. Crucially, we perform these measurements in both real space and redshift space, the latter accounting for the peculiar velocity distortions that affect observed galaxy positions and are unavoidable in actual survey data.

## Results and Implications

Our analysis reveals that the reduced 3PCF exhibits only small differences when galaxies are separated by luminosity or color. These modest variations are fully consistent with observational measurements from major galaxy redshift surveys, including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS). The weak dependence on galaxy properties suggests that the shape-related information encoded in the 3PCF is remarkably robust across different galaxy populations.

The close agreement between our model predictions and the observational data carries important physical implications. Specifically, it lends strong support to the straightforward association of galaxies with CDM halos and subhalos, without requiring complex or finely-tuned prescriptions for how galaxies populate their dark matter hosts. This validates the subhalo-based framework as a physically motivated and observationally consistent method for modeling the galaxy-halo connection, and demonstrates the power of higher-order clustering statistics as a test of galaxy formation models within the LCDM paradigm.

# The Lambda-CDM Model and Its Validation Through the Sloan Digital Sky Survey

## Introduction

The Lambda Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) model stands as the standard cosmological framework describing the origin, structure, and evolution of the Universe. Often referred to as the "concordance model," LCDM successfully explains a wide range of astronomical observations, from the cosmic microwave background to the large-scale distribution of galaxies. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has played a pivotal role in testing and refining this model, providing some of the most comprehensive observational data in modern cosmology.

## Understanding the LCDM Model

The LCDM model rests on two fundamental components that together account for approximately 95% of the Universe's total energy density:

- **Lambda (Λ):** Representing dark energy, this component is associated with the cosmological constant and drives the accelerating expansion of the Universe. Dark energy constitutes roughly 68% of the cosmic energy budget.

- **Cold Dark Matter (CDM):** This non-baryonic, slow-moving matter interacts primarily through gravity and makes up about 27% of the Universe. It provides the gravitational scaffolding necessary for the formation of galaxies and larger cosmic structures.

The remaining 5% consists of ordinary baryonic matter—the atoms that form stars, planets, and living organisms. The model assumes a Universe that is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales, consistent with the cosmological principle.

## The Role of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey

Launched in 2000, the SDSS represents one of the most ambitious astronomical mapping projects ever undertaken. Using a dedicated 2.5-meter telescope at the Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, the survey has systematically imaged large portions of the sky and measured the spectra of millions of celestial objects.

### Key Contributions of SDSS

The survey has generated detailed three-dimensional maps of the Universe, revealing the intricate cosmic web of galaxies, filaments, and voids. These observations have provided critical tests for the LCDM model in several ways:

1. **Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO):** SDSS measurements of these primordial density fluctuations serve as a "standard ruler" for measuring cosmic distances, confirming predictions of the LCDM framework.

2. **Galaxy Clustering:** The statistical distribution of galaxies observed by SDSS matches the patterns predicted by cold dark matter simulations.

3. **Redshift Surveys:** By measuring the redshifts of millions of galaxies, SDSS has mapped the expansion history of the Universe with unprecedented precision.

## Conclusion

The synergy between the theoretical LCDM model and the observational power of the SDSS exemplifies the modern approach to cosmology. While the LCDM model continues to face challenges—including tensions in measurements of the Hubble constant and questions about the fundamental nature of dark matter and dark energy—it remains remarkably successful. The wealth of data provided by surveys like SDSS ensures that our understanding of the Universe will continue to deepen, potentially revealing new physics that could refine or transform the current cosmological paradigm.

The galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) encodes valuable non-Gaussian information about the large-scale structure of the Universe that is inaccessible through two-point statistics alone. However, accurate theoretical predictions of the 3PCF remain challenging due to the complex, nonlinear relationship between galaxies and their underlying dark matter distribution. In this work, we present a framework for predicting the galaxy 3PCF using high-resolution cosmological N-body simulations combined with a subhalo abundance matching (SHAM) approach to populate dark matter halos and subhalos with galaxies. We measure the 3PCF across a range of triangle configurations, scales, and galaxy number densities, systematically characterizing its dependence on halo occupation and the connection between luminous and dark matter tracers. Our results demonstrate that the inclusion of subhalos significantly improves the modeling of small-scale clustering and the shape dependence of the 3PCF compared to models based on halos alone. We further quantify the sensitivity of the 3PCF to cosmological parameters and galaxy-halo connection assumptions, showing that the combination of two- and three-point statistics can break degeneracies between cosmology and galaxy bias. We validate our predictions against measurements from mock galaxy catalogs and assess the impact of sample variance and configuration selection on parameter constraints. These findings highlight the 3PCF as a powerful and complementary probe for extracting cosmological information from upcoming galaxy surveys, and provide a robust simulation-based methodology for its interpretation.

---

*Keywords:* large-scale structure, three-point correlation function, cosmological simulations, dark matter halos, subhalos, galaxy-halo connection, higher-order clustering

We investigate the validity of the local bias model as applied to the three-point correlation function using high-resolution dissipationless N-body simulations of a flat ΛCDM cosmology. Local bias posits that the galaxy density field can be expressed as a Taylor expansion in the underlying mass density field, δ_g = b₁δ + (b₂/2)δ² + ..., such that higher-order clustering statistics inherit a characteristic dependence on the linear and nonlinear bias parameters. We construct mock galaxy catalogs by populating dark matter halos identified in our simulation volume, allowing us to measure both the two- and three-point correlation functions across a range of scales and to compare directly with the predictions of the local bias framework.

On smaller, nonlinear scales, however, we find significant departures from the local bias prescription, indicating that the mapping between galaxy and mass density fields cannot be fully captured by a simple deterministic, local relation. We quantify the scale at which these deviations become important and assess the systematic biases introduced when inferring b₁ and b₂ from the hierarchical amplitude under the assumption of local biasing.

Our findings have direct implications for the interpretation of higher-order clustering measurements from galaxy redshift surveys and for efforts to constrain cosmological parameters and galaxy formation physics through the three-point correlation function. We discuss the limitations of the local bias approximation and comment on the necessity of incorporating nonlinear and stochastic contributions when modeling galaxy clustering on small scales.

# Abstract

We investigate the dependence of the reduced three-point correlation function (3PCF) on galaxy luminosity and color using a suite of high-resolution N-body simulations populated with galaxies via a halo occupation distribution (HOD) framework. The reduced 3PCF, $Q(r_{12}, r_{13}, \theta)$, provides a sensitive probe of the nonlinear gravitational clustering and the morphology of large-scale structure that is complementary to lower-order statistics such as the two-point correlation function. By constructing volume-limited samples spanning a range of luminosity thresholds and color cuts, we quantify how galaxy properties modulate both the overall amplitude and the configuration dependence (shape) of $Q$ across scales from $\sim 1$ to $30\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$.

We find that brighter galaxy samples exhibit systematically higher values of $Q$ on small scales, reflecting their preferential occupation of more massive halos and enhanced nonlinear bias. The configuration dependence of the reduced 3PCF—characterized by its "U-shaped" anisotropy as a function of opening angle $\theta$—becomes progressively flatter for the most luminous samples, consistent with stronger filamentary alignment in high-density regions. Splitting by color, we show that red galaxies display a markedly larger 3PCF amplitude than blue galaxies at fixed luminosity, indicating that color-dependent galaxy assembly bias imprints a measurable signature on higher-order clustering that cannot be fully captured by adjusting the linear bias alone.

We compare our measurements to predictions from local and nonlocal biasing models and demonstrate that a linear-plus-nonlinear deterministic bias prescription fails to simultaneously reproduce the amplitude and shape of $Q$ for all subsamples, particularly on quasi-linear scales. Our results underscore the importance of the reduced 3PCF as a discriminating diagnostic for galaxy formation physics and galaxy–halo connection models, and highlight the need to marginalize over higher-order bias parameters when extracting cosmological information from galaxy surveys. We discuss implications for the analysis of upcoming spectroscopic datasets, where joint modeling of two- and three-point statistics can break degeneracies between cosmology and galaxy bias.
